subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
passage: I'm Shankar's older cousin, Uday. Yesterday Shankar, almost two, wanted the wooden elephant on the top shelf. He didn't try to climb. He pointed at it, looked at Paati and said, "Uh, uh!" qa.a: On the top shelf.

qa.a: He was using her arm as his way of reaching the toy.

qa.a: Wait and call for an adult, since climbing toward a high shelf is unsafe at his age.

qa.q: How does Paati feel about being used as a tool?
qa.a: Amused; she laughs and happily helps. 😊

subtype: Approach: trial and error [Action]

subtype: Approach: bargaining over roles [Action]
passage: Joseph and Vasudha, both five, grabbed the toy stethoscope at the same moment in the colony garden in Kochi. "I'm the doctor!" "No, I'm the doctor!" Vasudha pulled. Joseph pulled harder. Then Vasudha let go a little. "Okay, you be doctor first. I'm doctor next game." Joseph thought, then nodded. "Deal." Vasudha lay on the bench as the patient, groaning dramatically. subtype: Approach: counting days left and dividing the chapters [Thinking]
passage: Varun, ten, sat on the veranda of his house in a small town in Sikkim with his Social Studies book and a pencil. The test was on Friday, four days away. He counted the chapters on his fingers: six. "Six chapters, four days," he murmured. "One a day is only four. So I need one and a half every day." He tore a page into strips and marked the book: Monday, chapter one and half of two; Tuesday, the rest of two and all of three. His friend Tenzin leaned over the wall. "Studying already?" "Just one and a half," said Varun. Suddenly the book looked much smaller.

qa.q: How many chapters did Varun have to study?
qa.a: Six chapters.

qa.q: What did Varun mean by just one and a half?
qa.a: He had divided six chapters over four days, so each day only needed one and a half chapters.

qa.q: What could Varun do if one day goes badly?
qa.a: Move the missed part onto the remaining days while keeping the Friday total in view.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see Varun's early start?
qa.a: Surprised, since the test is still four days away.

grounding: It shows a child counting days and chapters and dividing the work into daily pieces.

subtype: Approach: counting days left and dividing the chapters [Thinking]

subtype: Approach: counting days left and dividing the chapters [Thinking]

subtype: Approach: working out what actually happened [Thinking]

subtype: Approach: values-first reasoning about interests [Thinking]
passage: "So, Science or Commerce?" asked her father, Lalit, at dinner. Rehana, fifteen, put down her spoon. "Everyone says Science." "And you?" "I don't know." Her mother tried another way. "When do you lose track of time?" Rehana thought. "Those data puzzles online. And debate club. I forget to eat." "And biology practicals?" Rehana laughed. "I watch the clock." Rehana stopped. "Wait. Data and arguing. That's basically what Economics is, isn't it?" Her father raised his eyebrows and nodded. "I think Economics fits me more than Science," she said slowly. Her mother nodded. "Then let's find out properly. Talk to your cousin who studies it." Rehana was already reaching for her phone.

qa.q: What activities make Rehana forget to eat?
qa.a: Data puzzles online and debate club.

qa.q: How did Rehana's thinking shift during dinner?
qa.a: From what everyone says is best to what makes time vanish for her, which pointed to Economics.

qa.q: What next step did her mother suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Talking to a cousin who studies Economics, to test the idea against real experience. 🙂

qa.q: How does Lalit seem to feel about the choice?
qa.a: Open; he raised his eyebrows and nodded, letting her reach the idea herself.

grounding: It shows a student asking which tasks make hours vanish, pointing to Economics over the expected Science route.

subtype: Approach: values-first reasoning about interests [Thinking]
passage: When I was choosing my stream in Class 10, everyone expected me to take Science. My cousins were all doctors or engineers, and my friend Jasleen had already filled her Science form. For weeks I felt confused. Then one night I made a list of when time disappears for me. It wasn't biology or physics. It was working out patterns in cricket statistics and arguing in the school debate. I realised I love data and argument. Economics suddenly made sense. My parents were surprised, but when I explained my reasons, they listened. I'm Manoj, I chose Economics, and I haven't been bored in class since.

qa.q: What did Manoj list one night?
qa.a: When time disappears for him.

qa.q: Why did Manoj feel confused for weeks?
qa.a: Family and friends expected Science, but he was not sure it matched what he loved. 😕

qa.q: What made his reasons convincing to his parents?
qa.a: He explained concrete interests, data and argument, rather than just saying he disliked Science.

qa.q: What would change if Manoj had just followed Jasleen?
qa.a: He might have ended up in a stream that bored him.

grounding: It illustrates a student reasoning from real interests rather than prestige to choose a stream.

subtype: Approach: values-first reasoning about interests [Thinking]
passage: School counsellor's note, Class 10. Varun, fifteen, came in anxious about choosing a stream. His father, Mr. Santosh, expects Science. Then he said, half to himself, "Numbers plus arguing. That's Economics, not Biology. In biology labs I just watch the clock." I had not mentioned Economics at all. He left saying he would research Economics and talk to his father with these reasons, not just feelings. He looked lighter walking out. Follow-up booked for next week.

qa.q: What does Varun do when nobody is making him?
qa.a: Debating, the stock-price game in the newspaper and logic puzzles.

qa.q: Why was Varun anxious?

qa.q: How did Varun reach the idea of Economics?
qa.a: He linked his own interests, numbers and arguing, to Economics himself; the counsellor only asked one question.

qa.q: How might Mr. Santosh react to reasons rather than feelings?
qa.a: He may be more open, since Varun can explain his interests clearly.

grounding: It shows a student reasoning from what absorbs him toward Economics rather than the expected Science route.

subtype: Approach: private and simple message [Action]
passage:

Swati

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: delaying until a fix is found [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Mr. Irfan,
I owe you an honest explanation and an apology. Two weeks ago, our team found a serious bug in your billing software. I chose to wait and fix it quietly before telling you, hoping to spare you worry. That was a mistake. The fix took longer than expected, and when your accounts team found the errors themselves, it looked as if we were hiding them. I understand why your trust in us has dropped. From today, I will tell you about any serious problem within one working day, even before we have a fix, along with what we're doing about it.
Sincerely,
Yash Mehra, Project Manager

qa.q: How long did Yash wait before telling the client?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What was Yash hoping for when he stayed quiet?
qa.a: To fix the bug quietly and spare the client worry.

qa.q: What approach would have protected trust better?
qa.a: Telling the client early, even without a fix, along with the plan to solve it.

qa.q: How did the silence look from the client's side?
qa.a: Like the team was hiding the problem, which hurt trust more than the bug.

grounding: It shows a manager delaying bad news to find a fix quietly, and trust suffering more than the delay would have caused.
